newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Air NZ unlikely to pay tax in 1996/7 June year.
newsitem.headline: Air NZ unlikely to pay tax in 1996/7 June year.

text.p: Air New Zealand Ltd gained a small tax credit in the first half and is unlikely to pay much tax for the full year to June 30, executives said on Wednesday.
The first half tax credit of NZ$593,000, compared with a tax charge of NZ$18.87 million in the 1995/6 first half, arose mainly from depreciation of aircraft.
Chief Financial Officer Bob Nazarian told a news conference the credit came mostly from timing differences on aircraft depreciation against book value, and from existing tax losses.
"Lower pre-tax earnings will be material because with our special tax depreciation rates on aircraft, the tax impost, as a rate, fattens up the higher your earnings go," Chairman Bob Matthew said.
Against that background, it was unlikely the company would pay much tax for the full year.
Air NZ earlier reported a NZ$76.74 million net profit for the half year to December, down 43 percent, and said the second half was unlikely to match the first.
It also said that in order to achieve planned cost savings of NZ$100 million over 1997/8, a one-off charge of around $25 million would be necessary in the current finacial year.
Asked if Air NZ was still likely to report a lower second half outcome if the NZ$25 million were removed, Matthew said: "It could well be".
He said the business over the six months had endured sharply higher exchange rates and high jet fuel prices.
About NZ$50 million had come off the result in exchange rate movement and $20 million in jet fuel prices.

"Serious money came off in six months on fuel, now you tell me what the interest rate scenario and what the exchange rate or fuel scenario will be then I'd be able to get somewhat closer for you," Matthew said.

"That's the dimension we are in and we felt that it was prudent to put a stake in the ground for the market place of our best guess, and our best guess is we are not going to match the first half year with the second," he said.
Much would depend on the extent to which the NZ$25 million came into account over the next few months, rather than in the 1998 financial year.
Matthews said Air NZ did not have an accurate fix yet of the total cost estimate related to "project save" as it would be incurred on a case-by-case basis.
